Self-study workbook

Agents 101

Seven modules. The chat-to-systems leap. Build real agents on your own company content.

Welcome to Agents 101

Want to see what Claude can make? Start with a file you’ll recognize as soon as you see it. Snake needs one message and none of your work files. Later you’ll make a briefing for your working week.

First steps

Using Claude Code or another tool? Switch the handbook to it

1 Ask Claude to make a game

Leave this handbook open. Open Claude Desktop and click New. If you see a Chat/Cowork switch, choose Cowork. Type this into the message box and press Send.

Type in Claude Desktop
Make me a Snake game and link to the file here.

In Claude’s reply Look under your message. The link to the Snake game is the file Claude made for you. Sometimes Claude opens the game board beside the reply as well. If you only get a description, ask “Can you attach the game?”

Once you see the game, come back to this tab and choose Keep my game to save it to your computer.

Make a folder for your game, then send the request below in a session using that folder.

2 Keep my game

Right now your game is in the conversation. Give it a home on your computer so you can open it again. The folder will hold the work you do here, including your calendar briefing.

Your computer
Windows folder walkthrough
  1. In File Explorer, open Documents. Click New, then Folder. Name it agents-101.
  2. In your game conversation, click + below the message box, then Add folder.
  3. Below the message box, click Project or folder, then Add folder. You can also find Add folder under +.
  4. In the picker, click Documents in the sidebar, then New Folder. Name it agents-101 and click Create, then Open. If you have the folder already, select it and click Open.
  5. In the picker, open Documents, select agents-101, and confirm your selection.

If Claude asks for permission, click Allow after checking that it names agents-101. When you see agents-101 attached to your message, copy and send this in the same conversation.

Prompt Cowork

Save the game we just made as `prework/snake.html` in the folder I added.

Wait for Claude to say it saved the game. Documents → agents-101 → prework is where you can find it again.

5 See what makes this an agent

Your game and your meeting summary were agent work. The agent took your request, used tools and saved files in your folder. What is an Agent names the five parts behind that in its short version.

Contents

  1. 01Getting GoingContext is how you paint by LLM. What you give the agent shapes what comes back, and you can go very deep with it: your profile, your rules, your judgement on the result.→
  2. 02Building Agent SystemsA system remembers, grows, and compounds around the one thing you need to make progress on. Chat can't.→
  3. 03Multi-Agent SystemsSeveral agents can work on one problem together. Split the work, run the agents in parallel, and let them hand off through shared files. Three agents search, three more decide. Handoffs are where work gets lost, so check them.→
  4. 04SecurityYou can't tell if your agent is safe from its output. Run a check; don't wait for certainty.→
  5. 05Catching HallucinationsThere is truth out there, and your agent's job is to stay connected to it. Where it cannot reach a source, it fills the gap: confident, plausible, wrong. Grounding, and checks you test on your own output, make the gap visible.→
  6. 06EvaluationsPut the Module 5 judge in a loop and the work improves by itself. The generator sharpens against the judge's feedback, round after round, while you walk away.→
  7. 07Agents Building AgentsAn agent can build the agent someone else needs. That is how you and the people around you learn faster.→

Getting Going

About 80 minutes. The course needs a paid Claude plan. Pro, the lowest paid plan, is enough.

Big Idea

Context is how you paint by LLM. What you give the agent shapes what comes back, and you can go very deep with it: your profile, your rules, your judgement on the result.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Engineer context
  • Write rules for an agent
  • Judge agent output

Start here

Start a fresh session or task at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

The question, to you: where did LLM output on your work come out generic, and what made it yours?

Keep that question in mind. Read the opening, Context is King, then do the exercise, Paint by agent with guardrails.

Lecture

Context is King

Ten versions, no spec

I approach almost all my work with agents now: broad analysis, a first version early, and far more text than I read line by line. Ten iterations is fine.

This autumn three colleagues started building an agent factory. I asked which capabilities they were building. They said they had a few problems to solve.

A colleague has a name for how I work: steering without reading all the text. For a while I felt I had lost a common language with people who write the spec first and meet to agree on it. Their meetings are how they iterate. Mine happen with the agent.

Antti Tevanlinna

What makes the difference?

The same question. Two answers. What makes the difference?

Same question, two answers

In one session, you ask "What is the capital of Italy?" Rome. "What should we have for dinner?" Italian: pasta, osso buco, risotto.

In the other, "What is the largest lake in Finland?" Saimaa. Same dinner question. Before you read on, guess what it suggests.

Finnish: salmon, rye bread.

The first exchange became context.

It reads the whole conversation every time

The LLM reads the whole conversation every time and generates the next response from all of it. Your first prompt and its answer are part of the input to the second prompt. Change the front, change the back.

That is context. You steer your agent with context.

Context is whatever you tell it

One more window. First prompt: "I'm a cardiologist preparing dinner for my patients." Then the same dinner prompt.

The suggestion shifts: heart-healthy, low-sodium, vegetable-forward. You told the LLM who you are.

Context is whatever you tell it: a fact, a role, a preference.

The first piece of the picture

Context is the first piece of the agent. Tools, goals, checks, boundaries and loops come later and run on it.

A file it reads every time

So far, the context was one message you typed, gone when the session closes.

You can put the context in a file the agent reads at the start of every session. You write it once, and it shapes every answer.

That's a guardrail. That's your turn.

Phase 2: Apply a framework you know

8 min

The site isn't there to sell. A colleague who visits it should think "this is the person I want to work with more, on the things they're great at."

Name the framework and tune it

StoryBrand answers "what kind of help is this person to others?" Its hero is the colleague, not you. Leave out its sales parts (Stakes, Call-to-Action).

Name the framework, tune it, have the agent run it. The LLM knows StoryBrand, so you don't need to list its questions. The same works for Toyota Kata or SWOT: "Apply X to Y, but tune for Z."

Keep yourself the protagonist, then run the beats

Applied to the whole site, StoryBrand would make the colleague the main character. This stays a personal site, and you stay its main character. Your name is the headline and your current work is front and centre. StoryBrand shapes only the section on how you help colleagues.

Prompt (Cowork)

Rework the section of my site about how I help colleagues, using Donald Miller's StoryBrand. The page stays about me: my name in the headline, my current work up front. Only this one section changes. A colleague who reads it should think: this is the person I want to work with more, on the things they're great at.

Use five beats: Character (the colleague), Problem (the work they're stuck on or want more of), Guide (why I'm their natural ally), Plan (what working with me is like), Success (what has changed for them a year from now). Leave out Stakes and Call to Action. Nobody is buying anything.

Ask me one beat at a time and wait for each answer. After the fifth, regenerate `module-1/site.html`, with the section written as prose in my voice, as sharp as my answers.

Phase 4: Anti-branding, the mirror

8 min

Most people can list what drives them mad at work in thirty seconds, but stall on what they're great at. Invert the easy thing. Define what you're for by inverting what you're against. Taleb calls it via negativa.

Name the framework, tune it, ask the agent to run it.

List what you hate, then invert it

List a few specific things you hate about work. Name actual things ("meetings where nobody disagrees," "decks where every page says 'iterating'"), not categories ("bureaucracy"). Vague input gives you a generic page again.

Prompt (Cowork)

Next comes a list of things I hate about work. For each one, work out what kind of work and what kind of people produce it, then describe me as the opposite, in the positive: what I do and what I move toward, never "I don't do X".

Use the result to sharpen how the whole site sounds: the headline, the first line, the section headings, the stance. Don't add a section about what I'm against. Then regenerate `module-1/site.html`.

After that you have a free hand on presentation. Rethink structure, order, sections and visual rhythm so that a colleague who opens the page wants to spend more time with me. Keep the substance we built: the section on how I help colleagues, the strengths, and the stance from this list.

Phase 5: Look back

6 min

The Debrief starts from the file the agent writes here. The agent asks you one question and waits for your answer.

Prompt (Cowork)

Look at the very first site you generated from just my LinkedIn profile, before I told you anything more. Find three specific claims you made in that version that turned out to be generic, empty, or wrong about me once we added real context. Name them and say why each one was generic rather than something true of me.

Then pick three lines from the current site that are most specifically me. For each, name the piece of context that produced it: my LinkedIn, my StoryBrand answers, my strengths, my hate list, or a call I made on a draft. Write both lists to `module-1/context-trace.md`. Before you save, ask me what I gave you that changed the page most, wait for my answer, and write it in my words as the last line.

LLMs go easy on their own output. If the three picks seem mild, ask the agent to flag more and be harsher.

Phase 6: Free iteration

6 min

Make it yours: color, layout, tone, a quote at the top, a section most sites lack. Iterate until you say "yes, this is me." You lead, with no set prompts.

Tip: steal a look and feel by naming a site. The LLM knows famous sites' design by name. Try "Restyle module-1/site.html to feel like X" with two or three sites, such as Stripe, Linear or Patagonia, and keep your favorite.

Phase 7: Close, package what you learned

4 min

Have the agent save what worked, so a fresh agent can do the same for someone else's bio.

Prompt (Cowork)

Write a rules file at `module-1/personal-brand-generation.md` that I can give an agent for the next personal-brand job: a colleague's bio, a team page, a client one-pager. Cover what it is for, the core rule (distinctive, not descriptive), what never to generate, what always to do, the moves we used (StoryBrand for the help section, the hate list turned positive for the voice, a borrowed look if we used one) and the voice rules. Take all of it from what we did in this session, the decisions and the reversals, not from general advice.

When you're done, summarize in 4–6 lines what's in the file: the structure you used, the strongest 2–3 rules, and anything you weren't sure about. Then tell me to open `module-1/personal-brand-generation.md` and inspect the first two or three rules before I accept it.

See the mechanism repeat in every phase

What happened:

In every phase the agent read everything in the session: your LinkedIn text, your answers, your strengths, the things you hate and the site it wrote last. The more specific the context, the more the output is yours.

Take the context move past this site

The point:

The LLM didn't get better between Phase 1 and Phase 6. The context did. The same mechanism works for business proposals, competitor analysis and product strategy.

This was Recipe 1. When the next output needs the same move, the Cookbook for Agent System Design holds the moves and components.

Lecture

Iterate and Learn

Context became something you can point at

Context is the bit you added that turned a generic About page into a site you recognise as yours.

The rules file keeps what context the agent needs, what generic looks like, what a stronger pass does differently, and which rule should survive into the next session.

Why the agent went easy on its own site

When the agent picked three generic claims in its own site, the picks were mild.

The LLM is tuned to be helpful and agreeable, and that holds when it grades its own work. A self-review is the same kind of output as the work it reviews.

The report is a hypothesis, not a result

Treat the agent's report as a claim about the work, not a verdict on it.

Where the report matches the session as you remember it, good. Where it doesn't, your memory of the session counts.

The agent generated, you decided

The site reads as yours because you knew the subject and corrected the drafts. Only you can catch a wrong line about you.

You act on the future to know what's real

You act on the future to know what's real. Nobody knows where agents are going, not Anthropic, not your board. The people who figure it out first run the experiment.

Mental models only come from doing.

Debrief

Five minutes. The agent reviews module-1/personal-brand-generation.md against the session and module-1/context-trace.md: what worked, what fell flat, what to keep, what to drop.

Ask the agent to review your rules file.

Prompt (Cowork)

Read `module-1/personal-brand-generation.md` and `module-1/context-trace.md`. Then re-read what we did building the site. Run a retro: which moves worked, which fell flat, where context broke through, where the output stayed generic. Compare the rules file to the actual work. Sort each rule into keep, sharpen, or drop. What's missing the rules should have caught?

Assume the rules file is at least 30% wrong or thin. Find that 30%. If fewer than two rules get dropped or substantially rewritten, say why before you proceed.

Then overwrite `module-1/personal-brand-generation.md` with the retro applied. Sharpen what's weak. Add what's missing. Drop what's wrong. Rewrite the file in place; don't append a "retro notes" section.

When you're done, list:
- dropped: rule text + reason
- sharpened: before -> after
- added: rule text + why the session needed it
- still uncertain: anything the rules should cover but you want me to weigh in on first

The agent updates the file and summarises the changes. Expect the generation rules to change a lot.

Push back on what the retro missed

The LLM is generous to a rules file it just helped write. Push back on anything that doesn't match your sense of the work.

Each round the agent turns the work into sharper rules and drops what the work disproved: do the work → capture → reflect → sharpen. Repeat on every rules file.

Get a cold read

Then get a cold read. Ask the agent to start a second, independent agent that sees only the site.

Prompt (Cowork)

Launch a fresh subagent to give an unbiased read on `module-1/site.html`. The agent should read it cold, with no memory of building it.

Have the agent answer:
1. Quote the one line that feels most uniquely this person (not the best line, the one most uniquely theirs).
2. Quote the most generic line that could be copy-pasted from anyone's site.

Where the critic calls a part generic, your context is thin there: add one sharp detail and regenerate the site. Where the critic's "uniquely you" pick matches your own view, that part works. Your view outweighs the critic's.

Key Concepts

  • Context is the brush: what you give the agent shapes the output.
  • Output got specific because the context did.
  • Guardrails are context you can reuse.
  • Your domain expertise is the test.

Bring to Module 2

Bring one live challenge: a decision you're making, a bet you're placing, or work whose direction is still unclear. Having it in mind is enough. Module 2 opens by pinning it down with the agent.

Pre-reads before Module 2

Optional: Karpathy's LLM Wiki post; Lindenberg's memory-architecture piece.

Lecture

Before the Memory

What you do:

Bring one live challenge. That is all Module 2 needs from you. The rest of this page is optional.

Module 2 works on real history: meetings, notes, decisions, half-written documents.

Bring one live challenge

Module 2 builds a memory: a folder of notes and source material the agent reads before answering. Bring a real challenge: a decision you're making, a bet you're placing, or work whose direction is still unclear.

Pick one open enough to need thought, narrow enough for 5-8 topic pages.

If stuck, scan your next two weeks of calendar; the biggest unresolved item is usually your challenge.

Check what the agent can read

Files on your computer are enough: documents, decks, exported pages, notes. Module 2 builds the memory from what you point the agent at.

Connectors are an optional extra. They link the agent to places where your work lives, such as a wiki or a shared drive. If one is already set up, the agent can use it. Module 2 does not wait for one.

Put a plan before action

Module 2 has the agent create and update multiple files. Ask it for a plan first, then approve or revise it. Runtimes offer this as a mode or via the prompt.

Use it when the next step may write several files or edit anything you care about. Skip it for quick one-turn work.

Pick one:

  • Ask the agent which planning control your runtime offers, then try it on a harmless file change.
  • Watch Matt Pocock's video about planning before execution.

Read the memory frame

Read Karpathy's LLM Wiki gist for the mental model: a useful system is a living pile of text the agent can read, maintain, and improve. Your memory starts as plain text, which the agent reads and rewrites easily.

Bring to Module 2: one live challenge. Module 2 opens by pinning it down with the agent.

End this session. Module 2 starts fresh at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Next

Your rules file already carries what you learned into the next session. Module 2 grows that into a memory for one real challenge.

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Building Agent Systems

About 90 minutes.

Big Idea

A system remembers, grows, and compounds around the one thing you need to make progress on. Chat can't.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Create agent memory
  • Create an agent
  • Schedule an agent
  • Review an agent's plan

Start here

Start a fresh session or task at ~/Documents/agents-101/. The new session does not see Module 1's conversation.

Your memory/, sources/ and agents/ folders are empty from prework, and you will not need Module 1's files. The agent writes your working rules in the Debrief. The existing root file only loads course navigation.

The question, to you: what's the difference between asking an agent a question and having an agent keep a knowledge base that every later agent reads?

Name the challenge you're carrying

Which challenge of yours isn't solved yet? Pick a challenge, not a task. You'll build a memory around it.

Suppose everything you've read and drafted on that challenge sat in a memory an agent could read and sharpen. What would change at work?

Connectors let the agent combine pieces that live in different places, such as a wiki page and an email thread.

Lecture

1st scheduled agent

One scheduled agent reads work context, follows one hard guardrail, and writes an output you can inspect. The context might be a calendar, a short note, or a file in the training folder.

The guardrail: propose or draft only, do not send, edit, book, or change anything. The schedule makes the agent run again without a fresh prompt and write the next result in the same place.

Exercise

Exercise: Name your next big challenge

Time: 15 minutes.

Session (new, "Module 2 - Building agent systems")

What you do:

Pick one real challenge before you build. The memory you build is a folder of notes and sources the agent reads before answering, and it needs one subject.

Pick your next big challenge.

Choose an initiative you own and are working on now, one that produces work: a memo, a plan, a decision, a brief, a campaign, a rollout.

Good: The Q2 pricing redesign: usage-based vs. seats, pilot cohort, sales briefing.

Not a fit: last year's re-org, becoming a better leader, understanding AI.

Write the brief.

The agent asks you three questions, one at a time, and writes ./challenge.md.

Prompt (Cowork)

I'm in a training where I'll build a working memory around one live challenge I'm wrestling with. Help me pin the challenge down. Ask me these in turn:

1. In one sentence, what's the initiative? A real, midsized-to-large piece of work you're carrying over the next few weeks: scope, stakes, still open.
2. What have you already tried, read, or decided? What's ruled out, what's still open?
3. Where are you currently stuck on this? What's the specific part you can't seem to get past, or the question you keep asking yourself without getting an answer?

When I've answered all three, write a one-paragraph brief to ./challenge.md. Show it to me before saving.

Exercise

Exercise: Build your challenge memory

Time: 47 minutes.

What you do:

Build a memory around the challenge in ./challenge.md: the board paper due in three weeks, the re-org you're shaping. Keep the challenge narrow enough that 5–8 topic pages cover it.

Keep the same session running. The empty sources/, memory/, and agents/ folders are in place from prework.

Phase 1: Curate, ingest, build

20 min

Phase 1 runs in three steps: the agent helps you plan which sources to use, saves each source or a pointer to it in sources/, then builds memory/ from them.

Always comply with your company's AI policy. Its rules on what can go through an LLM hold here. If in doubt, check before uploading.

Ease yourself in. Bring only what you'd share with a smart assistant without a second thought. If a thread, deck or doc feels sensitive, skip it.

Approve the plan before the files change

Several steps here re-read sources/ or memory/ and rewrite many files. Ask the agent for a plan first.

If the agent starts reading before it shows the plan, stop it, narrow the task, and say "continue". For something simple, set a limit: "10 sources max".

Curate the source plan

Step 1. Curate. The agent checks which sources it can reach and asks where your material lives.

Prompt (Cowork)

I'm building a knowledge memory for one specific challenge I'm working on. Do this in three steps:

1. Check what connectors are enabled right now. Name the ones you can reach (wiki, docs, storage, chat, email) and the ones that would be useful but aren't connected.

2. Then ask me where my work material lives: my team's wiki (whatever the tool), my shared drives and docs, email threads, chat channels, personal notes, favourite practitioner blogs. Get specific: tool names, the 2–3 most relevant spaces/folders, the people I've been talking to about this challenge.
   Ask one question at a time. Wait for my answer before asking the next. Do not show me the question list.

3. Then propose a curation plan covering three kinds of material: (a) internal knowledge: which searches in which tools, (b) recent work: which threads, folders, decks, (c) outside-in: 2–3 working practitioners or specific articles worth reading (not vendor blogs).

Two rules for the plan. First: only recommend sources I would feel comfortable sharing with an LLM today. If something is likely to be sensitive (board material, personal emails, customer data, HR records), flag it as "skip for now" and leave it out of the plan. Second: curate only the paths and spaces I actually name. If you spot nearby material I didn't name (a sibling folder, other files in the same drive), list what you see and ask before including any of it. Never pull it in on your own. I'll push back where the plan is off.

Ingest the sources

Step 2. Ingest. The agent saves the content of each source in sources/.

What the agent reads. The CLI agent reads any path you name; use absolute paths outside the training folder.The desktop agent reads files you attach; attach outside sources before sending.The agent reads your selected working folders; add a folder or attach a file for one message.

Prompt (Cowork)

For every source in the curation plan we just agreed, create one file in sources/. Use the best method per source:

- Publicly fetchable URL (practitioner blog, public article)? Fetch the page, save the text as sources/<slug>.md with a header naming URL + title + why-it's-relevant.
- Reachable via a connector you have (wiki, docs, drive)? Pull the content through and save the same way.
- Local file on my laptop at a path I named? Save sources/<slug>.md as a reference: absolute path + title + why-it's-relevant, no copied content. You'll read the actual file directly when you build the memory.
- Behind a connector you can't reach, or in a tool you don't have? Save sources/<slug>.md as a reference too: URL or path + title + why-it's-relevant + "not reachable: share with me when you want this included." Don't ask me to paste anything; if I want it included, I'll share the file.

Create files only for the sources in the plan we agreed. If you come across other material while you work (files I didn't name, a folder you weren't pointed at), don't add it; note what you saw and I'll decide whether it belongs.

When done, tell me the three lists: (1) fetched and saved as content, (2) linked by local path, (3) not reachable, waiting for me to attach. I'll attach whatever I want to include before we build the memory.

- Behind a connector you can't reach, or in a tool you don't have? Save sources/<slug>.md as a reference too: URL or path + title + why-it's-relevant + "not reachable: share with me when you want this included." Don't ask me to paste anything; if I want it included, I'll share the file.

Create files only for the sources in the plan we agreed. If you come across other material while you work (files I didn't name, a folder you weren't pointed at), don't add it; note what you saw and I'll decide whether it belongs.

When done, tell me the three lists: (1) fetched and saved as content, (2) linked by local path, (3) not reachable, waiting for me to attach. I'll attach whatever I want to include before we build the memory.

The agent reports three lists: saved as content, linked by local path, and not reachable. Aim for 8–10 items across the first two. The third list is usually empty. To include an item from it, share the file with the agent.

Build the memory under a plan

Step 3. Build memory. Ask the agent to write a plan first and wait for your approval before it changes files.

Prompt (Cowork) ⟦M:plan⟧

Read every real-content file in sources/. For each major topic you find, create a markdown file in memory/ with a clear title, 3–5 key claims, and an "open questions" section for things the sources disagree on or leave unclear. Then write memory/index.md that links to every topic page with a one-line description.

Rules:

1. Sources first, always. Every memory page derives from real content: either a sources/ file with content inline, or a sources/ reference file that links to a local path (read the linked file directly when you need it). Skip sources/ files marked "not reachable" and any empty placeholder files. If no real content is reachable yet, stop and tell me before writing anything in memory/.

2. Every claim ends with a citation in the form `[sources/<filename>]` pointing to the file it came from. One claim, one source file, on the same line. If a claim has no source, don't write it; put the gap in "open questions" instead. I'll spot-check citations against the files.

3. Distinctive, not descriptive. Extract what's specific to my situation: my company, my sources, my challenge. If a claim could appear in a competitor's memory on the same kind of problem, it's too generic; rewrite or cut.

Phase 2: Your first custom agent

10 min

A custom agent is a markdown file of instructions: what the agent is for and which rules it follows.

Prompt (Cowork)

Help me create my first custom agent as a markdown file in agents/. Ask me these one at a time. Wait for my answer before asking the next. Do not show me the question list.

1. What recurring job should this agent do for my challenge? One sentence, e.g., "draft a next-step memo for my CEO," "surface three risks for next week's stakeholder meeting," "synthesize three talking points on progress so far."
2. What rules matter? Starter rules: cite the memory file for every claim, never invent, ask when a source is thin, keep my voice. Change at least one so it's actually mine. Include any hard lines: things the agent must not do even if asked.

Pick a filename from the job. Show me the file before saving.

Phase 3: Compound

7 min

A good memory gets sharper as new sources arrive, not longer.

Pick one source that fills a gap: an article, a doc you skipped, a local file. Paste its link or path after the New source: line.

Prompt (Cowork)

Take the source below and integrate it into the memory. Steps:

1. Read the source. Integrate its claims into existing pages (sharpen, don't append). Drop any claim the source contradicts. For new topics, add pages in the existing shape. Update memory/index.md.
2. Rewrite tops in place. Replace old framing; don't preserve it above a new section.

When you're done, tell me three pages that got sharper (not longer) and one claim that got dropped or replaced.

Phase 4: Let it maintain itself

4 min

Prompt (Cowork)

Review the memory for real problems of three kinds: contradictions between topic pages; claims that need a source pointer but don't have one; older pages that likely went stale given what's in the newer sources. Also check that index.md links every page in memory/.

Report up to six, real issues only. If a category is clean, say so and move on. An empty category is a valid finding, not a quota to fill. For each, propose a specific fix and rate severity: high (would mislead a decision), medium (missing signal), low (cosmetic).

Of the issues you found, name the one you're least sure is real and say why. That's the one I should scrutinize first.

Don't apply anything yet. Ask me to approve or reject each one.

Phase 5: Close, put it to work

6 min

Ask your memory the hardest open question on your challenge, not "summarize the sources." For example: "What's the strongest argument for option A over option B?" "Where does our current plan break if the market shifts?"

Your question gets two answers: one from a helper agent in an empty folder, the way a chat answers, and one from the agent you built in Phase 2. Both go side by side into module-2/close.md. Type your question after Question:.

Prompt (Cowork)

Answer my question below twice and save both answers in module-2/close.md, under the headings Bare and System.

1. Bare: dispatch a helper agent in an empty scratch folder with only the question. No memory, no rules, no files.
2. System: run the question through the agent I built in Phase 2, using my memory and its rules, citing the memory file each claim came from. Mark any line that used the source I added in Phase 3.

End close.md with one line: what the System answer has that the Bare one could not. Then add the gap the System answer still left to the open questions of the memory page it belongs to.

Take stock of the system you built

What happened:

A memory is files you keep, not a thread you close.

The point:

A system is persistence (files the agent reads again) plus automation (instructions the agent follows without you retyping them). Together they compound: each cycle starts from what the last one left.

This was Recipe 2: sources, memory, rules file. For your next challenge, the Cookbook for Agent System Design holds the same moves.

Lecture

Compounding

In Phase 3, new sources made the existing topic pages sharper instead of longer. The second batch of sources improved what the first batch built. A chat cannot do that. That is compounding.

A few problems, or a capability?

We started building an agent factory. Three people went off and deployed agents, fast. I asked what capabilities they were building. They said: we have a few problems to solve.

Solve a problem and close it, and problem four costs what problem one did. Keep what each one taught in files the next session reads, and problem four starts ahead. That is the difference between a chat and a system.

Stop chatting. Build a system.

I keep repeating this. In a chat you handhold the agent, take a few actions, and at the end nothing is saved. Your performance is about the next hundred sessions, not this one.

A system is persistence plus automation

A system has two parts:

  • Persistence. Files on disk the agent reads again, not a thread that resets.
  • Automation. The instructions sit in a file the agent reads at session start.

A saved document with no agent is just a document. An agent with no files is a chat. Together, the system keeps getting better the more you feed it.

Why the sharpening happens

The agent read the existing topic pages first, then the new sources, and then rewrote the pages. Where an old claim and a new source disagreed, the weaker claim was cut. Context shapes output, as in Module 1, now across a whole folder.

It gets better by being edited

Keep the rules small and boring. Apply them consistently across thousands of small updates, and let the compounding do the work.

A folder of text, and that is the point

The memory is a folder of markdown files. No database, special tool or paid tier is needed.

The agent in agents/ is also markdown: instructions a session reads when you point it there. Any agent runtime can read it.

Language models are strongest at reading and writing text. Knowledge stored as text is knowledge the agent can read and update directly.

Three layers, one folder

Three layers, separate on purpose. Raw sources: the untouched originals you dropped in. Memory: topic pages the agent maintains and sharpens. Rules file: the instructions the agent reads so every update follows the same pattern.

Sharpen the memory, never the sources, or you lose the evidence.

What this unlocks

The agent's answers cite your files and sound like your company, not like a generic industry take. Generic AI becomes your AI when you build the memory it reads.

Could a competitor claim this?

If a competitor could have written a page, the memory is growing but not compounding. Spot what's still generic and sharpen it.

It can only use what someone wrote down

The agent works only from what is in its context: the session and the files it reads. Most of what you know about your company sits in heads and corridors, and nobody has written it down.

Every round moves one more piece of that knowledge out of your head and into files the agent reads next session.

Debrief

Five minutes. The agent reviews the session and writes your own working rules for this directory: the rules every agent here reads, drawn from what worked, what went wrong and what you had to repeat.

Prompt (Cowork)

Review this session and write the first version of CLAUDE.md at the training-directory root. The evidence: ./challenge.md, every file in sources/ (scan titles + first lines), every file in memory/, and our conversation.

The rules file governs how agents behave in this directory from now on: how memory gets compiled, how sources are treated, what claims require citations, what counts as "specific to my challenge" vs. generic. Every rule you write should be traceable to a specific moment in the session where the rule either helped or would have helped.

Write them as standing rules, not as the story of this session. Cover at minimum: the memory (when and how pages get written, what grounds them), the sources (what they are, whether they're editable), the agents (how they relate to the memory), and anything else the session showed we need.

Push back on the summary

Push back on anything in the agent's summary that doesn't match your sense of the work. "Keep the draft I accepted as an example, beside the fixes." "You missed the bit where we had to regenerate three times because of X."

Look for what the agent left out. A summary that names three rules and skips the messy part, where you had to ask twice, is missing the rule you need most.

Fix the output, then fix the rule

Your agent is "right" when it works. If the same miss comes back when you ask again, the agent lacks context: sharpen the memory, tighten a rule or rewrite the prompt. You find the next mistakes by using the system and watching where it goes wrong.

Finding a miss and fixing its cause is continuous improvement, done by hand.

The model will change under this

The model will be replaced. Your memory stays.

Your folder holds your challenge, your sources and your rules. A better model reads your folder better.

Key Concepts

  • A system compounds around your challenge: each new source sharpens what is already there. A chat starts from zero.
  • A system is persistence plus automation.
  • Three layers in plain text: untouched raw sources, a memory the agent sharpens, a rules file.

Bring to Module 3

Bring your challenge memory. In Module 3, several agents work on it. Set up the scheduled agent now and it reads the memory every morning while you go on. Module 3 does not wait for it.

Exercise

Exercise: Your first scheduled agent

Time: 35 minutes to set up. Then one glance each morning.

What you do:

Put a scheduled agent in front of your memory. Each morning it reads the memory and tells you something useful.

Pick one of three jobs:

  • Morning plan: reads memory and calendar, writes a 5-line plan naming which meetings move the challenge and which are noise
  • Daily risk scan: reads memory, flags the assumption most likely wrong or the question open longest
  • Next move: reads memory, drafts one action: a message, a question, or a small decision for today

Pick the one you would read tomorrow morning.

Phase 1: Connect any data the job needs

8 min

For the morning-plan job, enable Google Calendar or Microsoft Outlook Calendar in your agent runtime's connector settings and sign in with your work account. Without a connector, use a calendar screenshot or exported agenda. The other two jobs need no connector.

Phase 2: Capture the look

7 min

Give your daily output the look of your company's website, or any site you like: colours, typography, headers, voice. The agent extracts the pattern into a plain-language style file on disk and reuses it by name, like the memory.

Prompt (Cowork)

Look at my company's website, or another site I name. I'll give you a URL or paste a key page when you ask. Extract the visual pattern: primary and accent colours (with hex codes), font families, header shape, spacing, overall tone of voice. Write it to ./style.md at the training-directory root, in plain language (not a CSS file). Short and practical: a designer reading ./style.md should be able to produce something that looks like our site without visiting it.

Then append one line to my root CLAUDE.md under a new "Styling" heading: "When producing HTML output, follow style.md."

Show me both files before saving.

Prompt (Cowork)

I'm setting up a daily agent that reads my challenge memory every morning and reports back as a stylised HTML page. Ask me, one at a time:

1. Which job: morning plan, daily risk scan, or next-move draft?
2. What should the output look like: how long, what sections, what voice?
3. What must this agent never do? Name at least one hard boundary.

When I've answered all three, write the file at module-2/morning-agent/morning.md. The output instructions say: write the result as a single self-contained HTML file to module-2/morning-agent/latest.html, following the styling rules in style.md at the training-directory root. Phase 4: Schedule it

6 min

Open the Schedule sidebar in the desktop app and click New task → New local task:

  • Name: Morning memory
  • Frequency: Daily at 7:00 AM, or the time you want it to fire
  • Prompt: the scheduling prompt below. It writes the daily output to latest.html.

Prompt (Agent workspace)

Read module-2/morning-agent/morning.md and run the job. Read the current state of memory/ as context. Follow the rules in that file and in the root CLAUDE.md. Write the output to module-2/morning-agent/latest.html.

Prompt (Agent workspace)

Save, run it once and open latest.html. It should look like your chosen site; plain default styling means the agent did not use the style file, so ask it to try again. To fix anything, tell the agent what to change, and it updates the instructions or the style file. The scheduling prompt names both files, so tomorrow's run picks up the change.

Phase 5: Let it run while you go on

4 min

The agent keeps running beside the course. Module 3 does not wait for it. For the first three days, don't retune. Open module-2/morning-agent/latest.html each morning and watch for:

  • Useful days: what made them work?
  • Comical or wrong days: what was missing from the memory?
  • Claims you, the domain expert, know are off: your next memory edits.
  • Styling drift from your company site: sharpen ./style.md.
  • Who else would read this output, and what would make them open it?

Turn the memory into a running loop

What happened:

Each morning's output shows what is sharp and what is soft in your memory.

The point:

A memory an agent reads on a schedule, producing output you respond to, is the start of a loop. Every HTML agent you build looks native to your organisation, because your CLAUDE.mdAGENTS.md points each agent to ./style.md.

Pre-reads before Module 3

Agent Trigger List, After Module 2, for noticing when work should call the agent. What is an Agent: tools, memory, context.

Exercise

Exercise: Prework before Module 3

Time: 40 minutes total. 25 reading, 5 noting takeaways, 10 on the helper-agent primer.

What you do:

Two reads. Neither asks you to build anything. Reading 2, on helper agents, takes ten minutes and Module 3 uses it. Reading 1 is optional background.

Reading 1. Five practitioners, automating their work.

See what a single agent already does for working practitioners who've folded coding agents into daily research, writing, and shipping.

Pick three. Read one piece each.

  1. Simon Willison. Browse his current coding-agent field notes. Pick one worked example where he shows the prompt, artifact, test, or correction rather than only announcing a feature.
  2. Edward Harker. Read his coding-agent operating notes (16 May 2026). Look for the operating routine around the agent, not a magic prompt.
  3. Armin Ronacher. Read The Coming Loop (23 June 2026). Notice what changes when the human designs the loop and its feedback instead of driving every step.
  4. Thariq Shihipar. Read The unreasonable effectiveness of HTML (20 May 2026). Track why changing the review artifact changes how closely the human stays in the work.
  5. Daniel Bilsborough. Read The Practitioner's Guide to Coding Agents (updated 6 August 2026). Look for the plain-text memory and the boundary where consequential work still needs a person.

For each pick, note in plain language: what is this person automating that they used to do by hand, and what's the move that made it work? Three bullets, one per practitioner.

The aim is to calibrate how much one agent can already do, so you know what coordinating three more buys you.

Reading 2. Helper agents, in plain language.

Module 3 Phase 2 spawns three helper agents in one session or task.

What it is. A helper agent is one the lead agent dispatches to do one focused job. It gets:

  • its own instructions (what it's for, what rules it follows);
  • its own context window (a clean slate, so its work doesn't clutter yours);
  • access to the same filesystem (it reads and writes in your working directory, same as the lead session or task).

When the job is done, the helper returns a single result to the lead agent and disappears. Several can run in parallel.

How to launch one. Ask the lead agent in plain language: "Launch a helper agent to review the three retrieval files and write its take to module-3/stances/planner.md." For several at once: "Launch these three helper agents in parallel," and list them. The lead agent waits for all three to return, then continues.

What you'll see. Your runtime shows a running task or agent entry with a short description for each helper. In Phase 2, each helper writes a stance file to module-3/stances/ as it completes.

What you don't need. No agent definition file and no special command. Plain-language prompting is enough for Phase 2.

For the full reference, open the Claude Code helper-agent documentationopen the Codex helper-agent documentationopen the GitHub Copilot subagent documentationopen the in-app help and search for agents. You're after the shape: helper with instructions, own context, returns a result. You summon it by asking.

End this session.

Next

When a task keeps coming back, have the agent build an agent for it. Pick by pain: a task you keep doing manually. Meeting prep and calendar triage are fine starters. Keep the first version proposal-only: the agent drafts, ranks, or prepares; you decide what leaves the system.

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Multi-Agent Systems

About 90 minutes. On a Pro plan this module may reach your usage limit. If it does, pause and pick up when the limit resets.

Big Idea

Several agents can work on one problem together. Split the work, run the agents in parallel, and let them hand off through shared files. Three agents search, three more decide. Handoffs are where work gets lost, so check them.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Orchestrate multiple agents
  • Split work across agents
  • Debug agent handoffs

Start here

Start a fresh session or task at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Today three agents search your documents and practitioner articles, and three more work out what the findings mean. Files on your computer are enough. A wiki or document connector is an optional extra.

Lecture

Agent that takes action

The scheduled agent runs with one new permission: post one message to a demo Slack channel.

The message holds no customer data, private names, commitments or decisions. The agent writes the message first and sends only after approval. If the channel is missing or the message needs judgment, the agent stops.

Writing a file changes your folder. Slack changes another system.

Exercise

Exercise: Name your crux

Time: 8 minutes.

Session (new, "Module 3 - Multi-agent systems")

What you do:

Ask the agent to read Module 2's memory/ and name the crux, Richard Rumelt's term for the one thing that, if solved, releases pressure on everything else. Push back when the first answer restates the problem.

Prompt (Cowork)

Look at my challenge memory. Find the load-bearing obstacle: the one thing that, if solved, unlocks the others. Richard Rumelt calls this the "crux."

Rules:
- Not a problem restatement. "We need to build credibility" is a goal, not a crux. "Prospects won't meet us until someone they trust vouches" is a crux: it names the mechanism that blocks everything else.
- Not a category. "Positioning is unclear" is a category. "Buyers can't tell in 30 seconds whether we sell training or consulting" is specific enough to act on.
- Test it: if this obstacle moved, would at least three other stuck things release? If not, keep looking. It isn't the crux.

One sentence. Save it to ./crux.md under a `## Crux` heading; show me before saving.

Exercise

Exercise: Three retrievers, one curator

Time: ~28 minutes.

Three retriever sessions fetch raw material on your challenge into sources/. A fourth session, the synthesizer, curates the material into memory/. All four read ./crux.md. Each session has its own context.

Two retrievers need nothing but your computer: internet, and docs on files you name. The wiki retriever is for a wiki connector you already have. Without one, leave it out. The synthesizer works the same from two files.

Keep your crux session as Session 4 (synthesizer). Open three more: 1 internet, 2 docs, 3 wiki.

In Cowork, keep your crux task as Task 4 and start three more: 1 internet, 2 docs, 3 wiki.

Paste each retriever prompt and confirm the short list the agent proposes. If an agent starts reading far too widely, stop it, narrow its task, then say "continue".

Session 1, internet: sources/internet-retrieval.md.

Prompt (Cowork)

No preamble. Propose your author list now.

You are the internet retriever for my challenge. Find practitioner-grade external material on ./crux.md (the crux and its ## Question section). No vendor blogs. No analyst predictions. Practitioners writing about their own work, last 6 months.

Then:
1. Propose 4–6 specific authors or recent articles worth reading. Ask me to confirm or replace any before fetching.
2. Fetch them.
3. Append each finding to sources/internet-retrieval.md as soon as you have it, what each practitioner says that's specific, with the URL, and one line on how their situation maps (or doesn't) to mine. Never overwrite earlier findings.
4. End the file with "Conflicts and gaps": where practitioners disagree, where my challenge is weirder than any of their cases, what the internet can't tell me.

Write each finding as soon as you have it; don't batch until the end. The synthesizer in another session reads `sources/` as you write.

No need to update `memory/`; another session is handling curation. Just write to `sources/`.

Sources first. Every finding cites the URL you actually fetched and the author. If a fetch fails or returns nothing useful, write "[NOT FOUND]", do not fabricate article titles, quotes, or author positions from prior knowledge.

Session 2, docs: sources/docs-retrieval.md. When it asks for clues, name files or a folder on your computer.

Prompt (Cowork)

You are the docs retriever for my challenge. Find the relevant recent documents and email threads for ./crux.md (the crux and its ## Question section).

Then:
1. Ask me for three clues: names of documents I remember, people I've been mailing about this, or drives/sites to check. My doc store is OneDrive / SharePoint / Google Drive / whatever my org runs; ask which. Use the clues.
2. Pull the content via the doc-store connector (OneDrive, SharePoint, Google Drive, whichever I use), or via files I've shared with you directly.
3. Append each finding to sources/docs-retrieval.md as soon as you have it, what documents and threads show, who said what, what's recent, what's decided, what's still open. Never overwrite earlier findings. Name where sources disagree; don't smooth over contradictions.
4. End the file with "Conflicts and gaps": disagreements between sources, things that should exist but don't, names conspicuously missing.

Write each finding as soon as you have it; don't batch until the end. The synthesizer in another session reads `sources/` as you write.

No need to update `memory/`; another session is handling curation. Just write to `sources/`.

Sources first. Every finding cites the specific document name (and path or URL) or email thread you actually opened. If you can't find a source for a claim, write "[NOT FOUND]", do not fill from prior knowledge. If a connector returns empty, say so; don't invent document titles.

Session 4, synthesizer: memory/.

Prompt (Cowork)

No plan or preamble. Enter the loop now.

You are the synthesizer for my challenge. Three retrievers are running concurrently in Sessions 1, 2, and 3. They'll write findings to sources/wiki-retrieval.md, sources/docs-retrieval.md, and sources/internet-retrieval.md as they finish. Your job is curation: integrate those findings into my memory/ topic pages, scoped to ./crux.md (the crux and its ## Question section).

Memory is curated, not a raw dump. Existing topic pages cover the challenge. Extend them where the new sources sharpen what's already there; create a new topic page where the retrievals reveal a topic memory was missing. Cite sources by filename + paragraph.

The loop:
1. Wait for any new content in sources/. When a file appears (or grows), read it.
2. Diff against existing memory/ pages. Extend in place if the topic exists; create a new page if it doesn't. Don't ask permission for either path.
3. Make the update. Cite the source file by name. Integrate, don't append. Keep claims tight.
4. Repeat until all three retrievals are integrated.

When all three retrievals are in: write a one-paragraph note at memory/_synthesis-m3.md. List each memory file you actually changed by name and the exact filenames git diff would show; if fewer changed than the retrieval count, say so explicitly. Name where retrievals contradicted what was already in memory by quoting the conflicting claims verbatim from each source. Flag the contradiction; don't smooth it.

Don't fabricate. Every memory update cites a source-file finding. If a retrieval is empty or thin, say so in your synthesis note rather than papering over the gap.

Exercise

Exercise: Three minds, one synthesis

Time: ~22 minutes.

What you do: Have three helper agents argue from different stances on your curated memory, then have one session decide.

Stay in the session that wrote ./crux.md, close the retriever sessions, and wait for memory/_synthesis-m3.md. If a helper reads too widely, stop it, narrow its task, then say "continue".

Ask the agent to spawn three helpers with different stances, then apply Rumelt's strategy kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions) to turn their notes into one answer in ./crux.md.

Prompt (Claude Code Desktop)

Spawn three subagents in parallel, each with a different stance. Each reads my curated memory/ and writes a short note (under 200 words) to module-3/stances/.

Subagent 1: Backward-from-end planner. Imagine the outcome we want in 12 months. Work backwards. What must be true by month 9, month 6, month 3, next week? What's the first move?

Subagent 2: Assumption experimenter. Roger Martin's test: for the most attractive option, what would have to be true for it to work? List the load-bearing assumptions. For each, name the cheapest test that could kill it within a week.

Subagent 3: Counterintuitive reframer. What's the obvious answer here? Now, what's the reframe? Question the framing of the question itself. Steal an analogy from an unrelated field. Which bias is operating, and what happens if we invert it? Be sharp, not glib.

When the three return, show me the stances side by side, unsummarised, so I read them as three voices. Tell me where memory had conflicts or gaps that weakened any stance.

Then synthesize. Apply Rumelt's strategy kernel: diagnosis (what's really going on, in plain language), guiding policy (one coherent approach that addresses the diagnosis), coherent actions (3–5 concrete moves that follow). Append only a new `## Answer` section to ./crux.md with Rumelt's three parts; do not modify existing sections. Name where the three stances disagreed and which one you sided with and why; don't smooth the disagreement. Show me before saving.

Lecture

Lecture: How agents work together

Six agents worked on one question in this module. Three searched, three decided. None of them talked to each other. They handed off through shared files.

Agents hand off through shared files

Each agent writes what it found to a file. The next agent reads the file, not the other agent's mind: sources/ held the search, module-3/stances/ held the three takes, crux.md holds the answer.

A file can be read later: by you, by another agent, by next week's run. A conversation between agents cannot.

Split the work, run it in parallel

Split the problem where its parts differ: a different source, a different dialect, a different stance. Give each part its own agent. Bring the parts back to one place that decides.

Three agents searched in parallel. Three argued from different stances. One session applied the strategy kernel and committed to one answer.

Two ways to run a team

Separate sessions. Each agent keeps its own context, tools and clock. You see each one work and can step into one without confusing the others.

Helper agents in one session. Quick parallel thinking with a bounded return. The main session starts each helper, gives it one job, and discards it when its file comes back.

A framework makes it pick

Without a framework, the synthesizer summarises three views, evenly weighted.

Hand the synthesizer the strategy kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions). The synthesizer then commits to one diagnosis and drops what does not serve it.

Handoffs are where work gets lost

Every split creates a handoff, and handoffs are where work goes wrong. A retriever finds two numbers and the curator keeps one. A source's internal shorthand is rewritten in public tone and loses its meaning.

Open the files where one agent handed to the next. An error made there stacks through the steps after it.

Split for a reason

Not every job needs a team. Could one prompt produce the same quality? Then write that one prompt.

Split where the parts cannot be one agent: different access, a different dialect, a different stance. One agent per recurring workflow; a team only where the workflow divides.

Lecture

Debugging Stuck Agents

Agents get stuck: wrong source, three views averaged into mush, the wrong file written, confident right before a failed handoff.

Diagnose before repair

Ask the stuck system to diagnose where the problem is: in the sources, in the processing, or at the boundary between agents.

Prompt (Cowork)

Find the root cause of this bug.

Read the relevant files and the recent session context. Tell me whether the failure is mainly:
1. a source problem: missing, stale, contradictory, or unread evidence
2. a processing problem: wrong prompt, wrong role, bad handoff, vague output shape, or synthesis that averaged away disagreement
3. a boundary problem: the agent tried to use data, tools, or authority it should not have had

Do not fix anything yet. Show me the failure chain in 5 bullets: what happened, where it started, where it became visible, what file or prompt caused it, and the smallest fix that would prevent the next run.

Adapt the prompt to your own system.

Sources, processing, boundary

  1. Sources: add the missing file, remove the stale one, split contradictory material so the agent sees the conflict.

  2. Processing: rewrite the prompt, role, handoff, or output format. Split an agent doing two jobs.

  3. Boundary: narrow the agent's job, remove the tool, add a human gate, move the risky step from "do" to "propose."

  4. Shrink the rerun: rerun only the smallest step that should now differ.

  5. Have the agent write the lesson: a rule for your CLAUDE.mdAGENTS.md on what to read first, what not to smooth over, which output format to produce, and when to stop and ask.

The review checks handoffs, not truth

The prompt asks the agent for a harsh review of the handoffs: at least two places where work was lost, each with evidence (the file, the step, what was lost). Without the demand for evidence, the review turns polite.

Push back on the summary

Push back where the summary is wrong: "The planner and the reframer needed to be separate." "The wiki retriever kept normalising before writing."

The briefing is still unchecked

Nothing checks the briefing yet, so whether it is right stays open.

Key Concepts

  • Agents work together through shared files: what one writes is the next one's context.
  • Split where the parts differ, run them in parallel, bring them back to one place that decides.
  • Two ways to run a team: separate sessions on shared files, or helpers the main session starts and discards.
  • Handoffs are where work gets lost: open the files where one agent handed to the next.

Pre-reads before Module 4

Agent Trigger List, After Module 3 and the multi-agent sections of What is an Agent.

Lecture

Reading: Before Module 4

Reading 1. Personal skills. A skill is a SKILL.md plus supporting files (policy text, templates). The SKILL.md says what the skill is for, when to use it, and how. The agent loads it when a task matches. In Module 4 you run your policy files raw, package the check with a policy lens and an agent-risk lens, then run it on your Module 2-3 system.

Reading 2. Agent risk sits on top of normal security. Network controls, access rights and audit logs still apply. Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound. Also watch secrets in context, tool confusion and skill supply-chain.

Before Module 4: jot three to five lines on what matters about the data you work with, e.g. "Sales never lets unredacted CRM exports leave the building."

After the optional check and pre-reads, end this session. Module 4 starts fresh at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Bring to Module 4: what's the worst thing it could do with that access?

An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.

Next

Until Module 4, keep working on your real problem: add an agent for a critical dependency, or a plan visualisation.

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Security

About 105 minutes.

Big Idea

You can't tell if your agent is safe from its output. Run a check; don't wait for certainty.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Audit an agent for security
  • Write a skill
  • Mitigate agent risk

Start a fresh session or task at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Today the agent reads the system you built in Module 3, your CLAUDE.mdAGENTS.md, and the policy files under module-4/policies/.

The question, to you: what would you want checked before this system works for a real stakeholder?

You write text. How does that text become actions in other systems?

The answers describe one mechanism. Each tool has a name, a description and an input format. The model picks the tool whose description fits the context and writes a structured request. The runtime turns that request into an action, and the tool does the work.

A tool call is text that becomes an action. If the tool description is vague, the context is misleading or the request goes to the wrong system, the action is wrong in the same way.

Exercise

Exercise: Run and package a security skill

Time: 40 minutes. Phase 1 ~10, Phase 2 ~8, Phase 3 ~22.

Session (new, "Module 4 - Security skill")

Start a new agent session at your training-directory root.Start a new Cowork task with your training-directory root as the working folder.

Name it m4-security-skill if your runtime supports session names.

What you do: Check your system from Modules 2-3 against the policy files directly, with no skill. Then package the check as one skill with two lenses: company policy and agent risk. You are done when the skill is saved.

A skill packages expertise (rules, checklists, steps) so the agent loads it when the work matches. You run the skill again instead of prompting again from memory.

Phase 1: Run the policies raw

10 min

The policies are in module-4/policies/: your company's own, or the Nordic-baseline reference. Ask the agent to check the system against them, with no skill yet.

Prompt (Cowork)

Read everything in module-4/policies/. Use those policy references to audit the agent system: the memory in memory/, the sources in sources/, the agent files in agents/, the root CLAUDE.md, and the multi-agent runs in module-3/stances/.

For each rule you can derive from the policy files, produce one row in a report: rule name, one-line description, verdict (compliant / violating / "I can't tell"), and one line of evidence from my actual files for that verdict. If you can't tell, say what evidence you'd need to decide.

If module-4/guess.md exists, put my guess at the top of the report, word for word. At the end, list the violating and "I can't tell" rows under my guess. Do not judge the guess; I compare.

Write the raw report to outputs/policy-report-raw.md. An "I can't tell" is a better answer than a confident guess.

Do not create a skill yet. This is the raw run.

Phase 2: Dictate what matters

8 min

You do not need to study the policy files first. Tell the agent what matters about your company's policies and your agent system.

Prompt (Cowork)

I want to turn the useful parts of outputs/policy-report-raw.md into reusable security expertise for the agent system: the memory in memory/, the sources in sources/, the agent files in agents/, the root CLAUDE.md, and the multi-agent runs in module-3/stances/.

Before you read or write any package files, ask me for 3-5 lines about what matters from my own head: the data, policy rule, customer, source, workflow, or failure mode I most want this reusable check to catch. Wait for my answer.

After I answer, read outputs/policy-report-raw.md and everything in module-4/policies/. Then propose the reusable package shape for my runtime and wait for me to steer.

Type three to five specific lines in plain language: the data your agent touches that would be a problem if it leaked, the rule your legal team cares about most, the customer your CEO would not want named in a transcript.

The agent then reads the raw report and module-4/policies/ and proposes what goes into the skill. Push back on anything that sounds like a generic GDPR brochure.

Phase 3: Author both lenses

22 min

The skill is a SKILL.md plus any reference files, with two lenses: company policy, and agent risk (what the agent can reach, what it might leak, what a misleading prompt or source might make it do).

Ask the agent to write both lenses and name the risk patterns the agent-security lens covers. Expect two short rounds of questions.

Prompt (Cowork)

Author the reusable security check now. Two lenses.

Build one reusable skill source under module-4/skills/agent-audit/. The main file is SKILL.md. It contains both lenses: POLICY and AGENT-SECURITY. Add supporting reference files only where useful.



Lens 1 - POLICY. Rules drawn from everything in module-4/policies/ plus the lines I just typed. For each rule, the lens produces one row in a report: rule name, one-line description, verdict (compliant / violating / "I can't tell"), one line of evidence from the target system. The verdict column stays plain - "I can't tell" is a real answer.

Lens 2 - AGENT-SECURITY. Check what the agent can reach, what sensitive material might stay in its context, and what could go wrong because ordinary text can act like an instruction. The lens covers these four risk patterns by name:

- prompt injection (direct - hostile input in a user prompt; indirect - hostile content in a retrieved source the agent reads)
- secrets in context and scrollback (API keys, customer data, partner-NDA material persisting in the transcript or the agent's working memory)
- tool confusion (agent invokes the wrong tool, or the right tool with the wrong scope, because the prompt or context misframes what to do: for example, the production-database connector firing when test would do, or the email-send tool dispatching when the user only asked for a draft)
- skill supply-chain (the skill itself, or any skill the agent loads, came from somewhere - who authored it, who reviewed it, what it can do)

For each pattern, the lens produces one or two specific risks in the target system, ranked, with one suggested agent mitigation per risk - scope, split, filter, gate, or review. These sit on top of normal company controls (network controls, identity and access management, logging, vendor/security review), not in place of them. Name that explicitly in the lens's preamble.

Before you save anything, grill me on missing details that can sharpen the lens or that would ruin the audit run. Ask no more than three questions in a round, wait for my answers, then ask one final round only if a load-bearing gap remains. Recommend the answer you infer where the files already point to one. Cover both lenses, especially the policy lens, which has no fixed list of risks to lean on.

After I answer, save the files. Keep the SKILL.md tight: when to use it, the two lenses it applies, the report shape each lens produces. Tell me what you saved: module-4/skills/agent-audit/SKILL.md and any reference files it needs.

For each rule, the lens produces one row in a report: rule name, one-line description, verdict (compliant / violating / "I can't tell"), one line of evidence from the target system. The verdict column stays plain - "I can't tell" is a real answer.

Lens 2 - AGENT-SECURITY. Check what the agent can reach, what sensitive material might stay in its context, and what could go wrong because ordinary text can act like an instruction. The lens covers these four risk patterns by name:

- prompt injection (direct - hostile input in a user prompt; indirect - hostile content in a retrieved source the agent reads)
- secrets in context and scrollback (API keys, customer data, partner-NDA material persisting in the transcript or the agent's working memory)
- tool confusion (agent invokes the wrong tool, or the right tool with the wrong scope, because the prompt or context misframes what to do: for example, the production-database connector firing when test would do, or the email-send tool dispatching when the user only asked for a draft)
- skill supply-chain (the skill itself, or any skill the agent loads, came from somewhere - who authored it, who reviewed it, what it can do)

For each pattern, the lens produces one or two specific risks in the target system, ranked, with one suggested agent mitigation per risk - scope, split, filter, gate, or review. These sit on top of normal company controls (network controls, identity and access management, logging, vendor/security review), not in place of them. Name that explicitly in the lens's preamble.

Before you save anything, grill me on missing details that can sharpen the lens or that would ruin the audit run. Ask no more than three questions in a round, wait for my answers, then ask one final round only if a load-bearing gap remains. Recommend the answer you infer where the files already point to one. Cover both lenses, especially the policy lens, which has no fixed list of risks to lean on.

After I answer, save the files. Keep the SKILL.md tight: when to use it, the two lenses it applies, the report shape each lens produces. Tell me what you saved: module-4/skills/agent-audit/SKILL.md and any reference files it needs.

Answer the questions, then sharpen the lenses

Answer the agent's questions briefly, then hand back the rest: "You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."

Ask the agent to show you where the skill covers each of the four named risk patterns. Ask for any that is missing. Make the rules sound like your company's policy, and keep the report narrow enough to read.

Escalate to a person when judgment runs out

Still not sure? Ask a person.

Sometimes the right next step is not another prompt. If the policy report still has a serious "I can't tell", or the security report names a risk you do not know how to accept, show the evidence to someone who owns that area: legal, security, IT, compliance, or the business owner. Bring the report, the files it quotes, the mitigation you applied, and the residual that remains.

The narrow question the expert can answer is sitting in the report. Walk in with that.

Separate prototype from production

Prototype vs production.

You did this for one risk. A production agent needs a check or a closed door wherever an action cannot be undone, and only a light check where redoing is cheap. You must do the work.

Take stock of the loop you ran

What happened:

Your Module 3 system now has three reports: the first policy report and one from each lens of the skill. You applied one mitigation and recorded one decision on the residual risk. Where your own judgment runs out, show the evidence to a human expert.

The point:

You will not get certainty. You run the loop: assess, mitigate, reassess the residual, decide. The reusable check is the expert in the room, and it carries to the next agent. The report holds the evidence and the decisions.

This was Recipe 4: the two-lens audit, four agent-risk patterns, five mitigations (scope, split, filter, gate, review), and "I can't tell" as a verdict. For the next agent, the Cookbook for Agent System Design names the moves and components.

Lecture

Lecture: The discipline of risk

You built something that works. Is it safe? Testing, policy and certification do not give agent systems certainty.

Classical security manages risk on predictable software

Classical software security is a risk-based practice, and the software it protects is deterministic: same input, same output. You find the bug, fix it, and check that the fix holds. That is why perimeter, access control and patching work.

Three things agents change

The behaviour is non-deterministic. Same prompt, same files, same tools, different session, different answer. One passing test is one sample.

Instructions are the attack surface. Ordinary English in a document your agent reads can make the agent decide to do something harmful with the access it has.

Capability is emergent. You can't fully predict what an agent's instructions, context and tools add up to. You can only set limits.

The result: safe enough, under these conditions, within these limits, for now. What may the agent read? What may it change? What must come back to a human?

Assess, then mitigate

The work is a loop of four plain, repeatable steps.

Assess. Check your agent against your company's rules, and package that check so you can run it again. The agent-risk lens asks what the agent can reach, what it can leak, and what ordinary text could mislead it into doing. Read the reports with judgment.

Mitigate. Pick one risk and apply the smallest change that reduces it: scope (give the agent less), split (two agents, different trust levels), filter (post-process output), gate (human approves) or review (a second agent judges).

Reassess the residual, then decide

Reassess the residual. Name the risk that remains and write it down: the residual risk is X; if Y happens, we made it less likely, not prevented it.

Decide. Accept the residual on record, or close the door.

"I can't tell" is a real answer. Closing it takes evidence, not a better guess.

The discipline is running the loop, not reaching certainty.

Now the move is to give it less

You have given the agent more: context, memory, more stances. Now give it less.

More context makes a good answer likelier. Less access makes a bad answer smaller.

Every door you close is a source the agent won't read; every tool you remove is a capability gone. Scope it down far enough and the system is safe and useless. You choose the point, name the risk that is left, and accept it on record.

The best mitigation is the door you don't open

The cheapest, most reliable way to reduce risk on an agent is to not open the door in the first place.

Should the agent have write access to that system? If not, scope down before you scope up. Should the agent read from that mailbox? If not, don't connect it. Should the agent draft customer-facing language? If that is where the biggest risk lives, a human drafts and the agent reviews.

Every door you don't open is a residual risk you don't have to name, mitigate or re-test.

Expect it to cost you a feature. It costs whoever sells you agents too, this training included: an agent that reaches less is a smaller thing to sell, and it is still the right call.

The discipline is what carries

Some of your agents will be wrong in ways you won't catch. The organisations that handle this well run the loop openly, name residual risks plainly, and close doors they don't need to open. Damn, this is complex stuff.

Read the reports. Pick a risk. Apply a mitigation. Name what's left. Decide.

Then run the check on the other agents you've built.

Build more skills for recurring work

A skill packages the how of a recurring judgment or workflow, so the agent repeats the method without you rebuilding it. Other examples: reviewing customer data use, preparing a weekly briefing, triaging a queue.

A skill works across projects and agents. Improve the skill where its method turns out thin.

To share, install the skill in a teammate's runtime. Their agent loads the same method by name, without your prompt history. A shared skill is not a deployed service, and sharing it does not settle who owns it.

Key Concepts

  • No certainty: assess, mitigate, reassess the residual, decide.
  • Anything the agent reads can instruct it, a source included.
  • "I can't tell" is a real answer.
  • Mitigations add to security controls, never replace them.
