Pre-reads before Module 5

Read Mata v. Avianca (2023) and the Deloitte Australia / DEWR report (2025) in the lecture.

Lecture

The Missing Check

What you do:

Read two public cases. In each, a court or a government record documents what the LLM produced and which organisational check was missing.

In both cases the truth was one lookup away. The LLM filled the gap with something plausible.

Case 1: Mata v. Avianca (S.D.N.Y., 2023)

A passenger's attorneys filed a brief that cited six cases. None of them existed. One attorney had found them with ChatGPT, then asked ChatGPT whether one of them was real. It said yes.

On June 22, 2023, Judge P. Kevin Castel fined both attorneys and their firm $5,000.

Read:

  • The sanctions opinion itself (readable, and it quotes Schwartz's affidavit directly): law.justia.com, Mata v. Avianca, Opinion and Order of June 22, 2023
  • CNBC's contemporaneous coverage for the shape of it: CNBC, Judge sanctions lawyers whose AI-written filing contained fake citations

Case 2: Deloitte Australia / DEWR report (2025)

Australia's employment department paid Deloitte A$439,000 for a review. Academic Dr. Christopher Rudge found references that did not exist and a quote falsely attributed to a judge.

The 3 October 2025 revision disclosed GPT-4o use, including for completing citations. Deloitte refunded the final installment. Rudge found new false references in the revision. The department replaced the report again on 3 February 2026.

Read:

  • The department's current report page and correction history: DEWR, Targeted Compliance Framework Assurance Review – Final Report
  • The released correspondence describing the approved toolchain, publishing uses, review, and missed errors: Department of Finance, FOI 25-26-084 Document 1
  • The Guardian's account, including Rudge's findings and the refund: Guardian, Deloitte to pay money back to Albanese government after using AI in A$440,000 report
  • The Register's technical summary, including the GPT-4o disclosure and the "new fake refs in the revision" detail: The Register, Deloitte to refund part of A$440k Australian report after AI snafu

Why the LLM fabricates

  • It completes the pattern. An LLM continues text in the form that looks right. A legal brief or consulting report calls for case names and citations, so they arrive whether or not the fact exists.
  • It fills gaps instead of stopping. When the sources miss a piece, the model supplies what makes the answer feel complete.
  • It verifies inside the same fiction. Asking the same model "are you sure?" is another fluent answer, not a check on the world. Verification has to leave the session and touch the source.
  • It inherits organisational shortcuts. If the workflow rewards speed, the fabrication survives.

Why grounding fails even when the facts are in context

  • The source is present but does no work. Buried under drafts and notes, a source sits beside a claim without supporting it. The LLM answers from the pattern the topic evokes.
  • The source says less than the answer. A file says one customer complained; the answer says customers are unhappy.
  • Conflict gets smoothed. Two sources disagree, and the LLM writes a clean synthesis. Grounded work keeps the disagreement visible.

Can you trust what the agent says inside its scope?

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Catching Hallucinations

About 85 minutes. On a Pro plan this module may reach your usage limit. If it does, pause and pick up when the limit resets.

Big Idea

There is truth out there, and your agent's job is to stay connected to it. Where it cannot reach a source, it fills the gap: confident, plausible, wrong. Grounding, and checks you test on your own output, make the gap visible.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Detect hallucinations
  • Benchmark AI checks
  • Build a judge

Start here

Session (new, "Module 5 - Catching hallucinations")

Working folder: ~/Documents/agents-101/.

The question, to you: which line in your Module 3 briefing reads almost right? Point at it.

Lecture

Lecture: Grounded, and four candidates to measure

There is truth out there

There is truth out there. Your sources carry shards of it. The LLM, left to itself, has no model of truth, only a model of what usually comes next in language that looks like yours.

When your sources support a request, the output is grounded. When they don't, the agent still produces something, and the tone looks the same.

Grounded means traceable to a specific file, number or quote in a source. A grounded claim can still be wrong if its source is wrong. Start with grounded.

Mostly right, ten times over, is mostly wrong

If an agent is 85% correct on a single step (an illustrative number), that sounds forgivable.

Ten unverified steps in a row (retrieval, synthesis, formatting, writing, checking, rewriting, summarising, publishing) at 85% each come to about 20% end-to-end: one task in five correct, four in five with a defect, usually where you won't see it.

A short loop (look up the order, check the policy, draft the reply) stacks little. A full workflow with no check compounds every miss.

The number doesn't tell you what will go wrong, only that something will. Design for that.

A test-and-fix loop collapses the error rate

Say your briefing is 10% fabricated, and a detector catches 90% of those claims. Fix what it flags, then test again.

Round 1: 10% → 1%. Round 2: 1% → 0.1%. Round 3: 0.1% → 0.01%.

The numbers are illustrative. Unchecked, errors compound against you. Checked against the sources every round, the fixes compound for you.

"Are you sure?" is another fluent answer

When you can't tell whether an answer is grounded, asking the agent "Are you sure?" returns another answer from the same source, in the same confident voice.

Large language models generate the next likely word, not the next true one. They are trained on confident, specific, fluent text, so they produce language that looks like that whether or not the material supports it. Fluency is not evidence, and the model cannot tell you which parts of its output are grounded.

Later models may fabricate less; the mechanism stays the same.

Steering without reading every line

I stopped reading full documents at work some time ago. I read to steer on a high level. Much of the text is for the LLM itself.

Grounding is what makes that safe. A line on my CV is a claim. You would check it against my work contract, not my LinkedIn profile. A check that goes to the ground lets you steer text you do not read.

Don't pick a method. Run the candidates.

Every grounding check misses something. Advice won't tell you what it misses on your material.

Run several checks in parallel on your own output. Four agents check the same 30 claims. A scorer measures each one for precision, recall and coverage.

Four candidates that fail differently

Each method tests a different link between a claim and its source.

1. Source triangulation. Does the claim appear in at least one source file? Catches invention.

2. Entailment. Do the sources support everything the claim says? Catches overreach.

3. Citation integrity. Does the cited source contain the claim? Catches citations that point at nothing.

4. Counter-evidence search. Does any source contradict the claim? Catches claims the sources argue against.

You have done this before

On the Mata v. Avianca pre-read, each method found a different gap:

  • Source triangulation: an unsourced "small firm" and an unsupported "ten minutes" estimate.
  • Entailment: a too-clean Schwartz timeline.
  • Citation integrity: a quote absent from the sanctions order.
  • Counter-evidence: CNBC blurring the $5,000 sanction.

The judge names its own limit

The winner, or the top two together, becomes a reusable judge file. The file names the method, why it won, and what it misses.

A groundedness judge catches invented content. It does not catch a wrong source, framing that tilts, what was left out, or a strategic call.

Check the text before it becomes an action

An agent action starts as text: a mail, a ticket update, a CRM change. Unsupported text becomes an unsupported action.

Have the agent propose. Check the proposal against sources or a judge. Then apply.

A drift signal, never proof

Run the same briefing prompt twice from the same sources, in two sessions. Compare what stays and what changes.

A stable claim can still be unsupported. Drift is a warning, not proof of fabrication. Two sessions give you a demo; the signal firms up at five to ten.

Exercise: Hallucination benchmark

Extract the claim pool

The agent extracts a varied pool of 30 claims from the briefing. Thirty is enough to start seeing the pattern.

Prompt (Cowork)

Open `module-5/briefing.md`. Extract 30 varied claims from the briefing, or every claim if it holds fewer.

Use short verbatim excerpts from the briefing wherever possible, so later detector findings can be matched back to the briefing. Include a mix of claim shapes:
- numbers or measurable outcomes
- named-entity claims
- quotes or paraphrases attributed to sources
- causal claims
- comparison claims
- recommendation or next-action claims
- claims that seem obviously grounded
- claims that smell like overreach

Phase 2: Run the four detectors

8 min

Four helper agents run in parallel on the same claim pool, each with its own detection method and output file. This step takes a while. If a helper agent reads far beyond the roster, stop it and narrow its task. If a helper checked only some of the 30 claims, ask it to cover the rest.

In your main session:

Prompt (Claude Code Desktop)

Run four detectors on `module-5/claim-pool.md` in parallel. Each detector is a subagent with a different method. Each reads `module-5/claim-pool.md`, `module-5/briefing.md`, `module-5/evidence-roster.md`, and the rostered evidence files named there. Each writes its findings as a list of claim-pool claims flagged, with one line of reasoning per claim.

Detector 1: Source triangulation. For every claim in the claim pool, check whether that claim appears in at least one file on disk. If no file supports it, flag it as ungrounded. Write to `module-5/detectors/source-triangulation.md`.

Detector 2: Entailment. For every claim in the claim pool, ask: does the briefing say more than the sources actually support? A source that says "one customer complained" doesn't support "the market is unhappy." Flag it as overreach when the briefing stretches what the source said. Write to `module-5/detectors/entailment.md`.

Detector 3: Citation integrity. Some claims in the claim pool will cite a source, either inline or implicitly. For each citation, open the cited file and check whether the file actually contains the specific claim attributed to it. Flag it as a broken citation when the citation doesn't back the claim. Write to `module-5/detectors/citation-integrity.md`.

Detector 4: Counter-evidence search. For every claim in the claim pool, actively look for evidence that contradicts it, not just evidence that supports it. Flag it as contradicted when disconfirming material exists in the rostered evidence that the briefing ignored. Write to `module-5/detectors/counter-evidence.md`.

One rule across all four detectors: quote each flagged claim exactly as it appears in `module-5/claim-pool.md`. The scorer uses strict substring match; paraphrased findings count as misses.

Spawn all four in parallel. When they finish, confirm that these four files exist: `module-5/detectors/source-triangulation.md`, `module-5/detectors/entailment.md`, `module-5/detectors/citation-integrity.md`, and `module-5/detectors/counter-evidence.md`.

Show me five claims from `module-5/claim-pool.md` with their numbers: a mix of shapes, at least one you would expect to be hard. Do not tell me your view of any of them.

Phase 3: Scorer runs the benchmark

20 min

A fifth agent, the scorer, scores the four detector files against the 30 claims:

  • precision: of what the detector flagged, how much was ungrounded?
  • recall: of the ungrounded claims, how many did the detector catch?
  • coverage: did the detector look at the claim pool?

Prompt (Cowork)

You are the scorer for a four-way detector benchmark. Your inputs:

- Claim pool: `module-5/claim-pool.md`
- Briefing: `module-5/briefing.md`
- Evidence roster: `module-5/evidence-roster.md` and the rostered evidence files named there
- Detector output 1: `module-5/detectors/source-triangulation.md`
- Detector output 2: `module-5/detectors/entailment.md`
- Detector output 3: `module-5/detectors/citation-integrity.md`
- Detector output 4: `module-5/detectors/counter-evidence.md`

Your job: adjudicate the 30 claims, score each detector against that adjudication, produce a scoreboard, name a winner.

First, create the reference adjudication. For every claim in `module-5/claim-pool.md`, label it grounded, ungrounded, or partly grounded. Quote the evidence line or file that supports the label. If you cannot find support in the rostered evidence, say so plainly. Save this reference set to `module-5/adjudicated-claims.md`.

For each detector:
1. Match detector findings to claim-pool claims by strict substring match. If you can't find the exact claim-pool phrase in the detector's output, count it as a miss. Do not reason about semantic similarity, do not paraphrase-match, do not accept "close enough."
2. For each claim, check whether the detector flagged it. If the adjudication says ungrounded or partly grounded, the detector should have flagged it. Count that as a hit. If the adjudication says grounded, the detector should not have flagged it. Count that as a false positive.
3. Compute precision (hits / total flagged) and recall (hits / total claims adjudicated ungrounded or partly grounded). Coverage = how many of the 30 claim-pool claims the detector looked at.
4. One line of qualitative notes: what this detector caught that others missed, what it missed, where its method is strong, where it's weak.

Save the scoreboard to module-5/scoreboard.md as a table:

| Detector | Precision | Recall | Coverage | Hits | False positives | Misses | Notes |

After the table, name one winner. "All four are useful" is not an answer. If top two are within 10% precision and 10% recall of each other, name the single winner first, then propose a two-method ensemble and say what each catches that the other doesn't. An ensemble is two methods at most.

At the bottom, add a one-line recommendation naming the detector or ensemble and the reason it won for output of this shape.

If `module-5/my-marks.md` exists, replace each `judge: -` there with your adjudication label, and add one line under the scoreboard table: on how many of those claims your adjudication agrees with my mark, and which ones differ.

Show me the full scoreboard table in chat after saving the file.

- Detector output 2: `module-5/detectors/entailment.md`
- Detector output 3: `module-5/detectors/citation-integrity.md`
- Detector output 4: `module-5/detectors/counter-evidence.md`

For each detector:
1. Match detector findings to claim-pool claims by strict substring match. If you can't find the exact claim-pool phrase in the detector's output, count it as a miss. Do not reason about semantic similarity, do not paraphrase-match, do not accept "close enough."

3. Compute precision (hits / total flagged) and recall (hits / total claims adjudicated ungrounded or partly grounded). Coverage = how many of the 30 claim-pool claims the detector looked at.
4. One line of qualitative notes: what this detector caught that others missed, what it missed, where its method is strong, where it's weak.

3. Return a short structured list: claim flagged, category, one-line reasoning.

Carry the benchmark pattern forward

The point:

You pick a quality check by running candidates on your own output and scoring them against your own reference. The winner becomes a judge you can defend. The pattern (candidates → benchmark → scorer → winner) works for any quality judgment you automate.

This was Recipe 5. The Cookbook for Agent System Design holds the moves and components.

Then show me the rules as they now stand in the file, the scoreboard row or claim behind each one, and the kind of claim you are least sure the judge catches.

Prompt (GitHub Copilot CLI)

Read `./AGENTS.md` if it exists, then scan `module-5/evidence-roster.md`, `module-5/claim-pool.md`, `module-5/adjudicated-claims.md`, `module-5/detectors/` (the four detector outputs), `module-5/scoreboard.md`, and `judges/groundedness-judge.md`.

Update `./AGENTS.md` so every later session checks its briefings with that judge. Add up to four short rules under "Groundedness checks": where the judge runs, and where the benchmark showed it cannot check. In those places the agent answers "not enough evidence". If the judge now covers an earlier rule, quote that rule and cut it. Write each rule so an agent that never saw this session can follow it.

Then show me the rules as they now stand in the file, the scoreboard row or claim behind each one, and the kind of claim you are least sure the judge catches.

Notice what the prompt insists on

The prompt tells the agent to change only the Groundedness checks section and keep every other section word for word. Without that limit, a small edit turns into a rewrite and earlier rules change.

The prompt also makes the agent re-read the section and confirm each rule is in the file. The agent's report says what the agent meant to do. The file shows what happened.

Push back on the summary

Correct the agent where a rule is vague: "name the evidence roster", "say when to stop and ask for sources."

Start with the misses that are costly and keep coming back: numbers in external notes, customer names in account summaries, policy claims in internal advice, citations in briefings. Have the agent write into your CLAUDE.mdAGENTS.md when the judge must run.

Propose, double-check, apply

An agent action starts as text: a mail, a ticket update, a CRM change. Wrong text becomes a wrong action.

For actions that matter, the agent proposes, the judge or a lookup in the source checks the proposal, and the agent applies only what passes.

Which check would let this action go without you?

Read What is an Agent, The autonomy ladder before you decide what the agent may do next.

A judge you have tested is enough for actions that can be redone. Where an action cannot be undone, an expert also reviews the proposal, the evidence and the judge's known limit.

Key Concepts

  • Grounded means traceable to a specific file, number or quote. Where the sources end, the agent keeps writing in the same voice.
  • Asking the agent "are you sure?" returns another fluent answer. A check has to touch the source.
  • The agent runs candidate detectors on your own output; you read the scoreboard and keep the winner.
  • The judge passed one benchmark. It names its own limit: wrong sources, framing and strategic choices stay outside it.
  • Reusable pattern: candidates, benchmark, scorer, winner.

Pre-reads before Module 6

Ethan Mollick, The Bitter Lesson versus The Garbage Can.

End this session once the judge is saved. Module 6 starts fresh in ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Next

You can spot ungrounded output with a judge. Next, the judge goes into a loop, and the work improves under its feedback without you at the keyboard.

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Evaluations

About 90 minutes. On a Pro plan this module may reach your usage limit. If it does, pause and pick up when the limit resets.

Big Idea

Put the Module 5 judge in a loop and the work improves by itself. The generator sharpens against the judge's feedback, round after round, while you walk away.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Run an eval loop
  • Steer agents with feedback

Start here

Start a fresh session or task at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

The question, to you: if you define the outcome and let agents find their own path, do they get better at your company's work, or is your organisation too messy for that? Ethan Mollick asks this in The Bitter Lesson versus The Garbage Can.

Run the loop without you in it

The judge checks every draft, and the agent turns each flag into a rule for the next draft.

Lecture

Evals as Steering

Ethan Mollick's The Bitter Lesson versus The Garbage Can sets two views side by side. In the first, you define the outcome, give the agent examples and feedback, and the agent finds its own path. In the second, a company gets its real work done through unwritten habits and workarounds, and an agent needs those mapped first.

You can check one agent's work yourself. You cannot check the work of every agent you run. An eval is your standard for good work, in a form the system keeps applying when you are not there.

Put an eval in a loop and the work improves: the agent writes, the judge checks, the agent rewrites its rules, and the next draft starts from better rules.

Your judge is the first kind of eval

You tested the Module 5 judge once, and it can now check any briefing.

Groundedness protects the floor

A groundedness eval protects the floor: every name appears in the source, every number traces to a file, every claim cites evidence or admits the gap.

Not enough.

Steering raises the ceiling

Two mails both stay grounded. One is forgettable. The other makes the reader act.

The better mail names the tradeoff and gives a clear next move.

A goal-nudger is a check for that quality: it scores each output on the quality you chose.

Groundedness protects the floor. Steering raises the ceiling.

A grounded mail can still be useless, so you need both.

Three rounds, nobody editing

The Module 5 judge goes into a loop.

In round 1 a helper agent writes a briefing. The judge scores the briefing and says what is wrong with each flagged claim. The main session turns that feedback into rules in ./generation-tactic.md. Rounds 2 and 3 follow the better rules, and the score improves with nobody editing.

You walk away. When you return, the agent's notes show each round's score and what changed. The judge never changed, so a better score means a better briefing.

The answer is never "the eval passed"

What would have to be true for this eval to be the right one?

The right eval checks the thing that matters, at the point where a mistake would hurt, against a standard you would defend. You decide which details the system must never miss.

The same check works for actions. An agent action starts as text: a proposed mail, ticket update, CRM change or command. A judge can check that text before it becomes the action.

Exercise

Exercise: The eval loop runs itself

Time: 45 min: first score ~5, walk-away ~30, read the notes ~10.

Session (new, "Module 6 - Evaluations")

What you do:

Start a loop: each round an agent writes your briefing again from better rules. Nobody edits a briefing by hand.

How the loop works. Each round, one helper agent writes a fresh briefing and a second helper agent scores it with your Module 5 judge. The main session turns what the judge flagged into rules in ./generation-tactic.md, the file the next writer follows. The judge never changes, so fewer flagged claims means a better briefing.

A typical result: 11 claims flagged in your Module 3 briefing, then 7, 7 and 4 over three rounds.

Phase 1: Score your Module 3 briefing

5 min

Ask the agent to score your Module 3 briefing with the Module 5 judge, then write the first rules in ./generation-tactic.md from what the judge flagged.

Prompt (Cowork)

Three things, in order.

1. Score my baseline briefing. If module-3/briefing-baseline.md is missing, stop and tell me. Otherwise dispatch a judge subagent that reads only these: judges/groundedness-judge.md, ./crux.md without its ## Answer section, memory/, and the ## Answer section of module-3/briefing-baseline.md. It writes module-6/runs/round-0/judgment.md, with claims judged and claims flagged on the top line.

2. If module-5/baseline-score.md exists, put its "Claims judged: N. Claims flagged: F." line beside today's count. Any difference on the same briefing is a first read of the judge's own noise; say how big it is.

3. Write ./generation-tactic.md from that judgment. It instructs a generator to produce a fresh one-page briefing on the question in ./crux.md, working from ./crux.md without its ## Answer section and from memory/. Give it one rule for each kind of miss the judge flagged, and have each rule name the miss it prevents. Keep it short enough that a generator will follow it.

Then tell me in five lines: claims judged and flagged in the baseline briefing, the earlier count beside it, whether the line I doubted in that briefing was flagged, the rule the judgment most clearly asks for, and one claim the judge could not check from the files.

Phase 2: Start the loop, then walk away

30 min

Ask the agent to run the loop: at least three rounds, until a round no longer improves on the one before.

Prompt (Cowork)

Run an eval loop using my fixed judge. Never edit judges/groundedness-judge.md.

Starting generation tactic:
- Read ./generation-tactic.md and module-6/runs/round-0/judgment.md from round 0. If either is missing, stop and tell me round 0 has not run.
- Create module-6/runs/round-1/, module-6/runs/round-2/, and module-6/runs/round-3/. If the loop continues, keep the same numbering pattern with round-4/, round-5/, and so on.

Run at least 3 rounds. After round 3, keep going until there is no longer significant improvement from the previous round.

For each round:
1. Dispatch a generator subagent. It reads ./generation-tactic.md, ./crux.md without its ## Answer section, and memory/. It writes the briefing for that round:
   - briefing.md in that round's folder
2. Dispatch a separate judge subagent. It reads judges/groundedness-judge.md, ./crux.md without its ## Answer section, memory/, and the briefing for that round, and nothing else. Give it no extra rules, checks or instructions beyond the judge file. It writes the judgment for that round:
   - judgment.md in that round's folder
3. The main session, not a subagent, reads the judgment for that round and any new lines in ./remarks.md, and rewrites ./generation-tactic.md for the next round. Integrate the lesson; do not append retro notes. `remarks.md` holds my own comments on the briefings. Use them when you rewrite the tactic, and never pass them to the judge. If there are none, carry on.
4. Starting after round 3, decide whether the last round improved significantly compared with the previous round. Significant improvement means a drop in flagged claims larger than the judge noise read in round 0, a new failure class resolved, or a clearly sharper generation tactic. When there is no longer significant improvement, stop the loop.

When the loop stops:
- Write module-6/eval-notes.md with:
  - a table of claims flagged out of claims judged, round 0 (the baseline briefing) first and then each loop round
  - the generation-tactic change after each round, naming any remark it came from
  - why the loop stopped
  - whether any judge subagent got instructions beyond the judge file
  - one thing the judge still cannot see
  - one human decision still needed
- In chat, show me the same summary in under 12 lines.

Do not stop for confirmation between rounds.

Starting generation tactic:
- Read ./generation-tactic.md and module-6/runs/round-0/judgment.md from round 0. If either is missing, stop and tell me round 0 has not run.
- Create module-6/runs/round-1/, module-6/runs/round-2/, and module-6/runs/round-3/. If the loop continues, keep the same numbering pattern with round-4/, round-5/, and so on.

Run at least 3 rounds. After round 3, keep going until there is no longer significant improvement from the previous round.

For each round:
1. Dispatch a generator subagent. It reads ./generation-tactic.md, ./crux.md without its ## Answer section, and memory/. It writes the briefing for that round:
   - briefing.md in that round's folder
2. Dispatch a separate judge subagent. It reads judges/groundedness-judge.md, ./crux.md without its ## Answer section, memory/, and the briefing for that round, and nothing else. Give it no extra rules, checks or instructions beyond the judge file. It writes the judgment for that round:
   - judgment.md in that round's folder
3. The main session, not a subagent, reads the judgment for that round and any new lines in ./remarks.md, and rewrites ./generation-tactic.md for the next round. Integrate the lesson; do not append retro notes. `remarks.md` holds my own comments on the briefings. Use them when you rewrite the tactic, and never pass them to the judge. If there are none, carry on.
4. Starting after round 3, decide whether the last round improved significantly compared with the previous round. Significant improvement means a drop in flagged claims larger than the judge noise read in round 0, a new failure class resolved, or a clearly sharper generation tactic. When there is no longer significant improvement, stop the loop.

When the loop stops:
- Write module-6/eval-notes.md with:
  - a table of claims flagged out of claims judged, round 0 (the baseline briefing) first and then each loop round
  - the generation-tactic change after each round, naming any remark it came from
  - why the loop stopped
  - whether any judge subagent got instructions beyond the judge file
  - one thing the judge still cannot see
  - one human decision still needed
- In chat, show me the same summary in under 12 lines.

Do not stop for confirmation between rounds.

Round 1's score arrives with nothing from you. Then open the newest briefing in module-6/runs/ and read it the way the person receiving it would. Add two or three remarks to ./remarks.md in plain words: "too hedged", "this number is not ours", "lead with the decision". Leave the loop running. The next rounds turn your remarks into rules. The judge never sees them.

What happened:

The notes list every round: how many claims the judge flagged, which rule changed before the round, and which of your remarks became a rule. Compare round 0, your Module 3 briefing, with the last round. Each briefing followed tighter rules than the one before.

Use these inputs; no preamble, start by writing the first generation tactic file:
Lecture

When the score stops moving

When flagged claims drop toward zero and stay there, the judge has stopped finding things. That does not mean the work is done.

A flat score is information about the judge or the work

Check both the judge and the work. The judge measures one thing: whether each claim is tied to the evidence. A grounded claim can still be vague or obvious, and this judge passes it.

The judge cannot see sharper framing, a recommendation that commits, or a briefing someone reads to the end. When the number stops moving, your judgment takes over.

Check every judge you intend to trust

Mark a few claims yourself and compare them with the judge's verdicts, as in Module 5. Where the judge passed a claim you would have sent back, the score is better than the work.

If the model stops fabricating, what is your judge for?

Your judge catches claims with no evidence behind them. Newer models may fabricate less, so this judge will find less. No model release so far has told anyone what good means in your company. That part is yours to define.

Lecture

The New Human Role in the Loop

Files hold what the agents know. Connectors bring material in. Agents read and write. Judges check. Loops make the next session better.

You do not disappear from this system. You move one level up: you design the loop and own the yardstick.

Which check would let the agent send the mail without you?

Would you allow your agent to send an internal mail related to what you do: a project update, a decision summary, a risk note, a stakeholder nudge?

What would have to be true before you let the agent hit send?

  • The mail sounds like it came from your world (Module 1).
  • The agent has the sources, the current facts and the open questions (Module 2).
  • The agent ran the right searches and weighed different views before writing (Module 3).
  • The agent has boundaries: what it can read, what it never says, which risks stay open (Module 4).
  • A groundedness judge ties names, numbers, claims and recommendations to evidence (Module 5).

Make many, pick the best, keep what won

In a loop that improves, something makes several candidates, something else picks, and what wins is kept.

The three stances in Module 3 and the four detectors in Module 5 made candidates. The groundedness judge and the goal-nudger pick. While you are away, the loop does both, and ./generation-tactic.md holds what won.

The human moves one level up

Today you stand between the agent and the world: the agent drafts, you inspect. That does not scale to many agents.

The new role is to design the loop: what the agent can reach, what it keeps, what stays fixed, what may change, what gets checked every time, what "better" means, and where a person still belongs.

For the internal mail, your answer may be draft only, review first, send to yourself first, or send automatically once the mail passes the groundedness judge and scores high on the goal-nudger. Some kinds of mail never go without a person.

Make a goal-nudger

Ask the agent to build one goal-nudger with you, for internal mail an agent could draft. A goal-nudger is an eval that scores one quality you care about and pushes the agent toward it. The agent saves it as ./goal-nudger-eval.md.

Prompt (Cowork)

Help me create a goal-nudger for internal mail I might let an agent draft or send. A goal-nudger is an eval that does not look for errors. It scores one quality I care about and pushes the agent toward it.

Groundedness is already checked by `judges/groundedness-judge.md`. This eval is for something else. It should push the agent to be better than it has to be on one quality that matters for my work.

Ask me at most three questions at a time and wait for my answers. For each round, recommend the answer you infer from my context so I can accept or correct it. Stop after two rounds: if we still cannot say how to score it, propose the narrowest version we can score and say what is left open. Start by offering examples I can choose from or adapt:

- executive crispness
- commercial sharpness
- specificity
- risk awareness
- actionability
- reader empathy
- strategic usefulness
- sounds like our team

If I choose a vague word, use the remaining question rounds to make it observable. For example, "strategic usefulness" might become: names the tradeoff, states a point of view, and gives the decision-maker a next move.

Once the dimension is clear, show me:

1. The dimension name.
2. A one-sentence definition.
3. Three examples: a 5/5 mail excerpt, a 3/5 mail excerpt, and a 1/5 mail excerpt.
4. The scoring rubric from 1 to 5.
5. What the eval should ask the agent to improve when the score is 3 or lower.

Then save the eval as `./goal-nudger-eval.md`. Show me what you wrote and ask for one final correction before saving.

I drifted too

When I built a module of this course with an agent, the rules sat in its context the whole time. In one session: five reversals from me on the agent's confident recommendations, four leaks of a banned word across three helper agents, and several times a "done" that was not done.

A check loop caught what the helpers missed. I caught what the loop missed. That is why the loop still has a person in it.

The better it gets, the less you watch

Every clean week is evidence that the loop works. Every clean week also gives you less practice at noticing when the loop stops working. If you design loops and never do the work inside one, you lose your eye for the work.

When did you last read one yourself?

No judge runs this check. Ask yourself: when did you last read one of the loop's outputs start to finish, without the agent summarising it first?

If that was a month ago, put a reading in your calendar. Read one output the way the person receiving it will.

The full picture, and what it is made of

The full picture is model, context, tools, goal, loop, checks, boundary and interface. For each part you decided what to give the agent and what to keep back.

Your role in the loop is to set the conditions for giving the system more autonomy, one loop at a time.

Push back on the summary

Push back on the agent's summary: "That rule is too vague, make it observable" / "you added a rule the file already had after round 2."

If the summary sounds too kind, check one removal: "You said you removed a rule. Quote the old line and show me it is gone from the file."

Key Concepts

  • The loop improves the work round after round with nobody editing. The judge never changes, so a better score means better work.
  • Groundedness protects the floor; steering raises the ceiling.
  • A flat score is information about the judge or the work. Check both.
  • You design the loop and own the yardstick.

Bring to Module 7

Tell the agent five moments at work when you would bring it in. The Agent Trigger List helps you spot them. Pick one where the eval loop's checks would let the agent work without you. The agent writes that trigger into module-6/trigger.md.

The Cookbook for Agent System Design and What is an Agent are optional references.

Once the trigger is written, end this module's session or task. Module 7 starts fresh at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Next

Your system now improves its own output. Next, it starts working for someone besides you.

Stopping here? Pause learning saves your place. Resume learning brings you back.

Agents Building Agents

About 45 minutes.

Big Idea

An agent can build the agent someone else needs. That is how you and the people around you learn faster.

What You'll Learn

After this module, you will be able to:

  • Have agents build agents
  • Improve an agent with an agent

Start here

Start a fresh session or task at ~/Documents/agents-101/.

Your system works for you because it reads your memory. Who is one person who could use what it makes, and what would they need if your memory stayed with you?

Exercise

Exercise: Build an agent for someone else

Time: 30 minutes.

Session (new, "Module 7 - Agents building agents")

What you do:

Your system works for you because it reads your memory. Pick one real person, describe an agent for what they need, and let an agent build it, judge it and rebuild it.

Describe the gap

5 min

Tell the agent four lines. It saves them as module-7/brief.md:

  • The gap: what your person needs and cannot get from your agent, because your agent reads your memory.
  • The job: what the new agent does, without your memory.
  • What it reads: files your person has, or files you would hand them. Nothing from your own memory/.
  • What it writes: one named file.

Over five minutes? Narrow the gap.

Have an agent build it

10 min

Prompt (Cowork)

Read module-7/brief.md. Build the agent described in it. Choose a lowercase hyphenated filename from the job, not the technology. State the exact path under `agents/`, then draft the agent file at that path.

The agent file must include:
- Role: one sentence on the job this agent does
- Rules: carry forward the rules my existing agents follow (cite the memory file for every claim, never invent, ask when a source is thin). Add rules specific to this agent's job.
- Inputs: the exact files or folders this agent reads. Paths, not descriptions. For PDFs or slide exports, include an extraction-depth check and flag any file whose body text was not actually extracted.
- Output: the exact file or shape this agent writes. If it's a report, name the filename. If it's a response, describe the shape.
- Hard lines: things this agent must not do even if asked.

Show me the file before saving. After I approve, save it to the exact path you stated, then run it once end-to-end on real input from my system. Report what it produced, where it hesitated, and where a source was thin.

Judge it, and the agent rebuilds it

10 min

Don't edit the new agent yourself. The judge checks the output against the files the new agent read, finds what fails, and the agent that built it rebuilds it.

Prompt (Cowork)

Run my Module 5 judge, `judges/groundedness-judge.md`, on the new agent's output, with the files the new agent read as its evidence and nothing else. Do not change the judge. Where the output fails, rebuild the agent you built so it passes, then run it and judge it again.

If the judge flags nothing, say so. Then check three claims you doubt against the input files yourself, and rebuild for what you find.

Take stock of the compound

What happened:

In under half an hour an agent built an agent for a gap a real person has, and rebuilt it until the judge passed it.

The point:

Each agent you describe is built faster than the last. When agents build agents for the gaps people around you hit, you and they learn faster.

The Cookbook for Agent System Design holds the moves for the next gap, under "agent generates agent".

Lecture

Lecture: Where is this all going?

Your agent can improve your agent

The eval loop rewrote a generation tactic from judge feedback while the judge stayed fixed. Point the same loop at one of your agents: its instructions, its skill, its checks.

The same loop can improve the agent that improves your agents, as long as the judge stays out of its reach. In Module 6 the loop never touched the judge file.

You described it; something else built it

The parts of an agent stay the same: context, a goal, tools, checks, a boundary, a loop. You decide each one. An agent assembles them from your description.

The agent that assembles them is itself an agent, so it can sharpen its own tools. The tool that builds tools compounds.

The parts hold; the model rotates

The parts are stable: context, tools, boundary, checks, loop, interface. What the model can do with each part moves with each model release.

The assembly is the durable half, and the assembly is what you spent your time on.

Every improvement is learning that compounds

A fix one agent makes to another stays on disk once a check has measured it. The next agent starts from it, and so does the next model.

What multiplies your work is how fast you and your organisation learn. Agents that improve agents speed up that learning as far as a check measures it.

Will your organisation learn faster than the model changes underneath it?

The model gets better on its own, for free. What your company knows about its own work gets better only when somebody writes it down and an agent builds on it.

If what your company knows stays flat, every model release widens the gap.

A flywheel, not a graduation

Everyone wants their 100 agents. From here, a hundred agents is a matter of describing them, one gap at a time, each checked like the first.

Name your next gap. Describe the agent for it. An agent builds it; you test it on your own work before it reaches anyone else's.

Key Concepts

  • Describe an agent and an agent builds it, then rebuilds it from what the judge finds.
  • The gap someone else hits is the brief for the next agent.

Everyone wants their hundred agents; the one that matters in six months is one nobody has thought of yet. What you take out of here is the ability to build it.
